title: Your ten verses
hookLine: pick the verses that stayed with you

cards: Some songs nobody ever sits down to memorize. They just stick, because at some point they meant something, and they come back at odd moments: in the shower, in the car, on a hard day.
A book of verses can work the same way. You've read four hundred twenty-three of them. Many will blur.
A handful may already have stuck, and those tend to come back when they're needed. Today is for finding them.

teach.h: CARRIED IN MEMORY, NOT ON SHELVES.
teach.b: The Dhammapada was made to be carried this way.

Tradition says the Buddha's teachings were passed on by heart long before they were written down, and a verse can still travel that way: learned as a child, heard in a teacher's talk, chanted at a festival.
Monks might learn the whole book by heart; a grandmother might know six verses and live by them. Both count. Here's a way to find yours.

First, walk back through the book in your mind. The twin verses: the mind comes first. Verse five, in Max Müller's English: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule."
Earnestness, and the island no flood can overwhelm. The fletcher straightening the arrow. The bee that takes nectar and leaves the flower.
The spoon that never tastes the soup. The deep, still lake. Conquering yourself, rather than a thousand times a thousand in battle.
Drop by drop, the water pot fills. The world seen as a bubble. Not to do evil, to do good, to purify the mind: the teaching of all the Buddhas.
Overcoming anger by not-anger. The Buddhas only point the way. The forest, the elephant, the creeper, the emptied boat, the lotus leaf.
Second, notice which ones tug at you: not the ones you think you ought to pick, the ones that came back on some ordinary day.
Third, write them down, in your own words if you like. There's no right list. Two people who read the same book will choose different verses, because they're living different lives.
A verse becomes yours when it has a job in your life.

how: Some Buddhists carry a few Dhammapada verses by heart rather than the whole book; teachers often give a single verse as a theme for reflection, and some people keep favorite verses written by a shrine or a desk.

practice: Breathe, and let the verses come to you rather than hunting for them; when one floats up, give it a small nod and let it settle back. Don't count, and don't judge whether it's a good one. Some will surprise you.

wordCard.voice: Dhammapada. Dhamma, the teaching, and pada, a step: the lines from this book that stuck, the ones with a job in your life, are yours.

carryVoice: Your line: yours. Ten verses, in any words, each with a job in your life. See you tomorrow.
